text_x: Pocket Bitcoin Says August Data Breach Affected Over 5,400 Customers Swiss Bitcoin financial services provider Pocket Bitcoin said an August security incident exposed data belonging to 5,120 customers, including names, addresses, bank transfer amounts and dates, and in some cases IBANs. A further 291 customers had more sensitive information exposed, potentially including identity documents, source-of-funds records, Bitcoin addresses and residential addresses. Pocket Bitcoin said its customer and transaction databases were not compromised, with the exposed data originating from bank correspondence and transaction lists stored in the affected support system. Bitcoin and private keys were not affected, and there is currently no indication that the leaked data has been misused. The incident has been reported to data protection authorities in Switzerland and Liechtenstein, as well as police. — link

However, stablecoins have still posted roughly $5.1 billion in net outflows from Binance year to date, while reserves across major exchanges have fallen by more than $16 billion. Darkfost said Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange by trading volume, now accounts for about 71% of stablecoin flows across exchanges. text_x: ARK Researcher Likens Ethereum to McDonald's, Solana to Chipotle and Hyperliquid to In-N-Out ARK Invest researcher Lorenzo Valente compared Ethereum, Solana and Hyperliquid to McDonald's, Chipotle and In-N-Out, arguing that the three networks represent fundamentally different L1 value-capture models. He said Ethereum has built crypto's most successful "franchise system" through L2s but charges too little at the settlement layer, while Solana retains more fees and MEV through a vertically integrated model. Hyperliquid has the shortest value-capture chain through tight vertical integration, no VC funding and fee-funded HYPE buybacks, though it faces greater concentration risk across products, team and revenue. — link

text_x: CFTC Moves to Dismiss CME Lawsuit Over Crypto Perpetual Futures The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission has asked a federal court to dismiss CME's lawsuit challenging its treatment of crypto perpetual contracts as futures. The CFTC argues that CME lacks standing because the same policy allows CME, the world's largest derivatives marketplace, to list digital-asset perpetual futures itself, meaning part of its alleged competitive harm stems from its own decision not to offer them. The regulator also said that even if the court reclassified perpetuals as swaps rather than futures, rival venues could still offer similar products, so the competitive harm claimed by CME would not necessarily be eliminated. — link
